The spec requires each row to have three cells: name, exit status, and output. The code writes: ``` {job['name']} {job['command']} {cache[job['name']]['output']} ``` The middle cell is `job['command']`, not the exit status. The captured exit status (`cache[...]['exit_status']`) is never placed in the report, so the report is incorrect. 2) The 0.25s start-spacing requirement is not met. The spec says 'start each later job at least 0.25 seconds after the previous job started.' The code sleeps only after a command finishes, and only when `ran > 1`: ``` if ran > 1: time.sleep(0.25) ``` Trace: the first job runs with `ran==1`, so no sleep; the second job therefore starts immediately after the first job finishes, with a gap equal to the first job's runtime (which can be well under 0.25s, e.g. `df -h /`). Only transitions from the 3rd job onward get any added delay. So the required minimum gap between the 1st and 2nd started jobs is not guaranteed. A correct implementation would delay before starting each non-first job (or track the previous start time). Additional concern (secondary, edge-case dependent): the cache is keyed solely by `job['name']`, while the spec describes matching records by both `name` and `command`. If two jobs share a name but differ in command, one record overwrites the other, so the cache would not contain a record for every job and the report would print the same output for both rows. With unique names (as in the example) this happens to work, but the report/timing bugs above already make the program functionally incorrect. Correct handling of stdout+stderr merge (`stderr=subprocess.STDOUT`, `text=True`), sequential execution, cache read/write, reuse counting, `Ran`/`Reused` line, and exit status 0 are otherwise fine.
